title: How 5,000 Sailors Eat, Shower & Sleep on an Aircraft Carrier
asof: Figures from US Navy reports 2006–2025 · sources in description

shots.s: More than five thousand people live on this ship.
For months, they don't step on land.
Jets land on the roof all night.
The bedroom sleeps a hundred.
The kitchen never closes.
So how do you eat,
shower,
and sleep,
on an aircraft carrier?
This is a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier.
It's one thousand and ninety-two feet long.
Two nuclear reactors drive it.
On top: the flight deck.
Below it: the hangar, full of jets.
And below that, decks and decks of people.
The crew of a carrier like USS Ronald Reagan: about fifty-three hundred, with its air wing.
For a lot of them, it's their first deployment.
On one Reagan deployment, about sixty percent had never deployed before.
Your bedroom is called a berthing.
Racks stacked three high.
Up to a hundred sailors can share one space.
You're so close that rolling over could wake the guy above you.
Your rack has a curtain.
It blocks the light.
It doesn't block the sound.
Day or night, you hear jets slamming down on deck.
The catapults fire,
and the slam rings through the steel.
People work every hour of the day here.
So someone is always sleeping, and someone is always waking up.
The galley on Reagan runs twenty-four hours a day.
It serves more than fifteen thousand meals a day.
Every month, about fourteen hundred gallons of milk.
Seven thousand pounds of lettuce.
And over thirty thousand pounds of chicken.
Not everyone can make it to mealtime.
So cooks make plates to go, for people on watch.
Before the USS Carl Vinson deployed in 2024,
eighteen semi-trucks lined up to fill its storerooms and freezers.
Food runs out.
So supply ships pull up alongside, at sea.
That's called a replenishment at sea.
Pallets swing across on cables.
Then everyone carries boxes down below.
On Vinson, even master chiefs carry boxes.
Then the cooks start all over again.
In the middle of the ocean, fresh water doesn't come from a pipe.
The ship makes it from seawater.
Its plants can make about four hundred thousand gallons a day.
The reactors need some of it.
So do jet washes, cooking and laundry.
And everyone wants a shower after work.
So sailors learn the navy shower.
Get wet. Water off.
Soap up.
Water on, rinse. Done.
When the plants break down, things shut off in order.
On USS George Washington, laundry closed first.
Then the dishwashing room.
Then showers get cut back.
The flight deck is right above some living spaces.
A Navy study put noise meters on a carrier for twenty-four hours.
During flight operations, living spaces below deck were very loud.
Each catapult launch ends with a hard slam.
That bang travels through the whole ship.
Sailors learn to sleep through it, or don't.
You never leave, so the ship has everything.
A gym.
A laundry.
A store.
And the sea, all the way to the horizon.
A deployment usually lasts months.
Then the carrier turns for home.
Families wait on the pier.
Thousands of sailors walk off the ship.
Your rack goes to the next crew.
Could you share a bedroom with a hundred people for months?
